summary: Defines the Content-Language header to indicate the language of content and the Accept-Language header for stating a preference. It is a standards-track document.

plainLanguage.summary: Many people would rather read information in a language they understand, and sometimes the same information exists in several languages or has to be converted into speech or Braille. This RFC defines the two headers that carry the language information needed for that: one naming the language of the content, one naming the languages a sender prefers.

questions: how to indicate language of content
how do q values work in accept-language
subtitle: Two small mail-style headers: one labels the language of content, the other states which languages you prefer.

tldr.problem: Information on the Internet is written in many languages, and a receiver needs to know which one before it can pick a version to send, translate it, or render it as speech or Braille.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines a 'Content-Language' header that labels the language of something with RFC 822-style headers, and an 'Accept-Language' header that states the sender's preferred languages, each optionally carrying a quality value.
tldr.outcome: Both headers carry language tags as defined in BCP 47, and both accept the older liberal grammar for backwards compatibility while requiring newly generated headers to use the current form.

facts.label: Quality value range
facts.value: 0 to 1, with up to 3 decimal digits

facts.label: Obsolete grammar
facts.value: Must be accepted, must not be generated

today: RFC 3282 is a Draft Standard published in May 2002. It obsoleted RFC 1766 and has not been obsoleted since. The headers it defines are still the standard way to label the language of content and to state a preference for one.

sections.title: Why Label Languages
sections.content:
There are a number of languages presently or previously used by human beings, and a great number of those people would prefer to have information presented in a language they understand. In some contexts it is possible to have information available in more than one language, or to provide tools such as dictionaries to assist in understanding a language.

In other cases it may be desirable to use a computer program to convert information from one format, such as plaintext, into another, such as computer-synthesized speech, or Braille, or high-quality print renderings. A prerequisite for any such function is a means of labelling the information content with an identifier for the language that is used in the information content, such as is defined in BCP 47.

This document specifies a protocol element for use with protocols that use RFC 822-like headers for carrying language tags as defined in BCP 47.
sections.plainLanguage: Both of the RFC's headers carry language tags, the short codes such as 'en' that identify a language. The first header says what language the content is in, the second says which languages the sender would rather have.

sections.title: The Content-Language Header
sections.content:
The 'Content-Language' header is intended for use where one desires to indicate the language or languages of something that has RFC 822-like headers, such as MIME body parts or Web documents. Its RFC 822 EBNF is Content-Language = "Content-Language" ":" 1#Language-tag, and the more strict RFC 2234 ABNF is Content-Language = "Content-Language" ":" [CFWS] Language-List with Language-List = Language-Tag [CFWS] *("," [CFWS] Language-Tag [CFWS]). The header may list several languages in a comma-separated list.

The CFWS construct is intended to function like the whitespace convention in RFC 822, which means that one can place parenthesized comments anywhere in the language sequence, or use continuation lines. A formal definition is given in RFC 2822.

In keeping with the tradition of RFC 2822, a more liberal 'obsolete' grammar is also given: obs-content-language = "Content-Language" *WSP ":" [CFWS] Language-List. Like RFC 2822, this specification says that conforming implementations MUST accept the obs-content-language syntax but MUST NOT generate it; all generated headers MUST conform to the Content-Language syntax.
sections.plainLanguage: The header holds one language tag or a comma-separated list of them. Older software sometimes put whitespace in odd places, so implementations must still accept that form even though they must not produce it.

sections.title: Examples of Content-Language Values
sections.content:
The RFC gives five examples of the header in use. A voice recording from downtown Liverpool uses Content-type: audio/basic with Content-Language: en-scouse, which is the local variety of English. A document in Mingo, an American Indian language which does not have an ISO 639 code, uses Content-type: text/plain with Content-Language: i-mingo, where the 'i-' prefix marks a language without an official code.

An English-French dictionary uses Content-type: application/dictionary with Content-Language: en, fr, followed by a comment explaining that this is a dictionary. An official European Commission document, in a few of its official languages, uses Content-type: multipart/alternative with Content-Language: da, de, el, en, fr, it. An excerpt from Star Trek uses Content-type: video/mpeg with Content-Language: i-klingon.
sections.plainLanguage: The examples cover a regional variety of English, a language with no official code, a two-language dictionary, a document in six languages, and a language invented for a film.

sections.title: The Accept-Language Header
sections.content:
The 'Accept-Language' header is intended for use where a user or a process desires to identify the preferred language or languages when RFC 822-like headers, such as MIME body parts or Web documents, are used. Its RFC 822 EBNF is Accept-Language = "Accept-Language" ":" 1#( language-range [ ";" "q" "=" qvalue ] ), and a slightly more restrictive RFC 2234 ABNF is Accept-Language = "Accept-Language:" [CFWS] language-q *( "," [CFWS] language-q ) with language-q = language-range [";" [CFWS] "q=" qvalue] [CFWS] and qvalue = ( "0" [ "." 0*3DIGIT ] ) / ( "1" [ "." 0*3("0") ] ).

A more liberal RFC 2234 ABNF definition is given as Obs-accept-language. As with the Content-Language header, conforming implementations MUST accept the obs-accept-language syntax but MUST NOT generate it, and all generated messages MUST conform to the Accept-Language syntax.

The syntax and semantics of language-range are defined in BCP 47. The Accept-Language header may list several language ranges in a comma-separated list, and each may include a quality value Q. If no Q values are given, the language ranges are given in priority order, with the leftmost language range being the most preferred language. The RFC notes that this is an extension to the HTTP/1.1 rules but matches current practice. If Q values are given, HTTP/1.1, RFC 2616, describes how to evaluate them.
sections.plainLanguage: This header lists the languages the sender would like, best first, or with a number between 0 and 1 after each one to show how strongly it is preferred.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The only security issue raised with language tags since the publication of RFC 1766, which stated that security issues were believed to be irrelevant to it, is a concern with language ranges used in content negotiation: they may be used to infer the nationality of the sender, and thus identify potential targets for surveillance.

The RFC calls this a special case of the general problem that anything you send is visible to the receiving party, and says it is useful to be aware that such concerns can exist in some cases. The exact magnitude of the threat, and any possible countermeasures, is left to each application protocol.
sections.plainLanguage: Saying which languages you read can reveal where you are from. The RFC leaves it to each protocol to decide whether that matters and what to do about it.

sections.title: Changes From RFC 1766
sections.content: Appendix A of the RFC lists the changes from RFC 1766. The definition of the language tags has been split, and is now RFC 3066. The differences parameter to multipart/alternative is no longer part of this standard, because no implementations of the function were ever found; RFC 1766 should be consulted for that information. The ABNF for content-language has been updated to use the RFC 2234 ABNF.
sections.plainLanguage: Compared with the version it replaces, the language tag definitions moved to a separate RFC, an unused multipart parameter was dropped, and the header grammar was rewritten in the newer notation.

viz.caption: The RFC 2234 ABNF for the Content-Language header
The RFC 2234 ABNF for the Accept-Language header

data.title: Accept-Language grammar
data.code:
Accept-Language = "Accept-Language:" [CFWS] language-q
                  *( "," [CFWS] language-q )
language-q = language-range [";" [CFWS] "q=" qvalue ] [CFWS]
qvalue = ( "0" [ "." 0*3DIGIT ] )
       / ( "1" [ "." 0*3("0") ] )
